newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iran, U.S. officials trade accusations in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Iran, U.S. officials trade accusations in Gulf.

text.p: Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said on Tuesday a senior U.S. official touring the region wanted to perpetuate tension between Iran and its Arab neighbours.
He was responding to remarks by U.S. Deputy Defence Secretary John White in Qatar on Monday warning Washington's Gulf allies that Iran was a potential threat.
"Maybe he has become angry because of what we have done during the last few weeks making more confidence-building between countries," Velayati said.

Velayati later left for Qatar while White arrived in Kuwait from Bahrain. The U.S. official had also been in Saudi Arabia which Velayati visited this week to invite Saudi Arabian King Fahd to an Islamic summit in Tehran in December.
The Iranian minister said: "This is for the benefit of peace in this region. Maybe they want, because this man is from the defence department, to sell their arms...

"If they say 'we are very happy to see that Iran and these countries are trying to make more confidence-building and have more cooperation' there is no justification to sell more arms to the people in this region," added Velayati.

He urged reporters to ask Arab states: "'Do you feel any threat from Iran'. I have not heard, specifically during recent weeks and months, from the people in this region that they feel some threat from Iran."

In December Iran's six Gulf Arab neighbours said at their annual summit in Qatar that Tehran's arms purchases exceeded its needs and called on international agencies to rid the region of weapons of mass-destruction.

Western diplomats say while Iran's ruling clergy have issued fiery criticism in recent weeks of Gulf Arab states for military links with the United States, Iranian diplomats have been trying to overcome the mistrust.

"Neighbouring countries feel that Iran is much more cooperative and from the other side we...say that we are not looking for conflict or superiority," said Velayati, who held talks on Tuesday with Kuwaiti leaders.
He reiterated a call for confidence-building by Gulf states through visits, bilateral and multilateral coordination and increased cooperation to reach joint security arrangements.

Such steps "are important elements for the regional cooperation for the security and this is a gradual thing. Since a few weeks ago we can hear the common voice in different parts of this region...that they want to have their security with cooperation among themselves," he added.
Iran, which has had rocky ties with most Gulf states since the 1979 Islamic revolution in Tehran, strongly opposes a military presence in the Gulf by outside powers.
